name: Al-Uqlidisi paper algorithms
summary: Al-Uqlidisi described doing Indian-numeral arithmetic with pen and paper instead of an erasable board, so working stayed visible on the page.
description: Pen-and-paper calculation procedures avoiding the earlier erasure operation; one described multiplication combines Indian operand digits with abjad-written intermediate products.
tier_reason: Prefer a bounded method tier over a platform-level one; the source expressly leaves later prevalence of the mixed-numeral procedure uncertain. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.

impact.note: Keeping the working visible on paper was a clear gain for regional calculators; direct descent of later paper arithmetic from this text is thin.

date.basis: Book IV of the work composed in 341 AH; the date belongs to the description rather than demonstrated widespread adoption.

events.statement: Pen-and-paper calculation procedures avoiding the earlier erasure operation; one described multiplication combines Indian operand digits with abjad-written intermediate products.
events.caveats: The passage describes a method, not universal displacement of dust boards or invention of paper. Abjad and Indian signs coexisted; the book is not a simple replacement story.

evidence.supports: Describes paper calculation and shows Indian and abjad signs within the same operation.

evidence.locator: Section 1.3, paragraphs beginning The earliest extant Arabic book and Al-Uqlīdisī's innovations
evidence.supports: Confirms no-erasure paper rules and cautions against assuming rapid uptake.

events.statement: The surviving manuscript of the treatise containing pen-and-paper methods was copied in July 1157.
events.caveats: Copying is not proof that the method was widely adopted; the author states reasons for moving away from dust boards, and uptake appears slow. The surviving witness supports access by its copyist; the copyist’s location and practical execution are not established.

evidence.locator: Chapter 1, PDF pp. 14–15, Yeni Cami 802 manuscript and work structure
evidence.supports: Dates the copy and identifies book IV as presenting paper methods.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 174–175, translation of multiplication example
evidence.supports: Identifies the distinctive written multiplication method.

links.statement: Al-Uqlidisi describes adapting board-style calculation to ink and paper without erasing, including a mixed-sign multiplication layout.
links.scope: Damascus, 952–953; Book IV compared with the board procedures discussed earlier in the same work.
links.alternatives: Erasable boards, wax tablets and other forms of reckoning remained alternatives.
links.caveats: This is an author-described technical adaptation, not an inferred personal sequence of experimental discoveries or a claim of broad deployment.
links.timing: Both nodes use the date of textual attestation; direction follows the explicit adaptation, not an invented earlier date for the board practice.
